metadata.summary: Recognize acute kidney injury early, evaluate competing and coexisting causes, apply current HRS-AKI criteria, and use vasoconstrictors with careful albumin, respiratory and transplant assessment.
metadata.application: Assess volume, infection, medications and kidney findings promptly; establish the likely AKI phenotype, begin indicated specialist treatment, and monitor response, oxygenation and volume while preserving the transplant pathway.
keyPoints: A small creatinine rise can meet AKI criteria; AKI does not establish HRS.
Current HRS-AKI assessment does not require routine albumin for 48 hours.
CKD and structural injury can coexist with HRS-AKI.
Individualize albumin and watch for pulmonary edema.
Use the US terlipressin day-4 dose algorithm and respiratory stopping rules.
Kidney improvement does not remove the need for transplant assessment.

bodies.heading: Explain the circulatory syndrome
bodies.body: Advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension can produce splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective arterial circulation despite ascites. Compensatory renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation contributes to renal vasoconstriction and impaired perfusion. Infection, bleeding, nephrotoxins and volume depletion can precipitate or worsen kidney dysfunction. HRS-AKI is one phenotype of AKI in cirrhosis with ascites; it may coexist with tubular injury or chronic kidney disease rather than being a guarantee of structurally normal kidneys.

bodies.heading: Recognize creatinine limitations
bodies.body: Low muscle mass can make a seemingly modest serum creatinine misleading. Compare with a reliable prior baseline and follow urine output and the clinical course. Current ADQI-ICA criteria recognize AKI with a creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise ≥50% known or presumed within 7 days, and/or urine output ≤0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 6 hours. A rise from 0.8 to 1.1 mg/dL in 48 hours meets the absolute-rise criterion even though the increase is only 37.5%. This establishes AKI, not its cause.

bodies.heading: Reverse correctable causes
bodies.body: Assess blood pressure and circulation, volume losses or overload, recent bleeding, infection and medication exposure. Stop nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs and reassess diuretics and other drugs that worsen perfusion according to current physiology. Treat infection and correct true volume depletion promptly; choose and reassess fluids from the clinical context. Urinalysis, sediment, proteinuria, kidney imaging and specialist assessment can identify obstruction or structural injury. Septic shock requiring vasopressors is strong evidence for another primary cause; infection without shock can also precipitate HRS-AKI.

bodies.heading: Use current HRS-AKI criteria
bodies.body: The 2024 ADQI-ICA consensus requires cirrhosis with ascites, an AKI trajectory, no improvement in creatinine and/or urine output within 24 hours after adequate volume resuscitation when clinically indicated, and no strong evidence that another process is the primary cause. Assess volume in every case. A routine 48-hour albumin infusion is no longer a prerequisite and is inappropriate in a euvolemic or overloaded patient. Pre-existing CKD or proteinuria does not automatically exclude superimposed HRS-AKI; evaluate possible mixed injury and revise the diagnosis as evidence changes.

bodies.heading: Pair vasoconstriction with individualized albumin
bodies.body: Once HRS-AKI is established, initiate specialist-directed vasoconstrictor treatment promptly with adjunctive 20% to 25% albumin when appropriate. Terlipressin is a preferred agent when the patient is eligible. A commonly recommended albumin amount during treatment is 20 to 40 g/day, but optimal dosing is uncertain: reassess volume daily, adjust to the patient and withhold albumin if overload or pulmonary edema develops. Albumin alone is not equivalent to vasoconstrictor treatment, and the HRS regimen should not be copied from SBP day-1/day-3 or paracentesis per-liter dosing.

bodies.heading: Choose alternatives in the right care setting
bodies.body: If terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated, norepinephrine with albumin is an alternative requiring ICU monitoring and central venous infusion in the consensus pathway. Midodrine plus octreotide with albumin is a less effective fallback when preferred treatment cannot be used and ICU transfer for norepinephrine is not possible. The review book lists this combination, but it should not be presented as an equally preferred substitute. Select the regimen with liver and kidney specialists, and monitor circulation, organ function and adverse effects.

bodies.heading: Use terlipressin safely
bodies.body: The US TERLIVAZ label applies to adults with HRS and rapidly worsening kidney function. Obtain baseline oxygen saturation and assess volume and acute-on-chronic liver failure severity. Do not start during hypoxia, including SpO₂ <90%, or worsening respiratory symptoms; ongoing coronary, peripheral or mesenteric ischemia is also a contraindication. Avoid use in ACLF grade 3. Creatinine >5 mg/dL is a limitation because benefit is unlikely, rather than a listed absolute contraindication. For highly prioritized transplant candidates, including MELD ≥35, benefit may not outweigh risk. Discuss fetal harm risk when pregnancy is relevant.

bodies.heading: Administer the US formulation correctly
bodies.body: For US TERLIVAZ, record the last available pretreatment creatinine as the dosing baseline. Give 0.85 mg IV every 6 hours over 2 minutes on days 1 to 3. One vial contains 0.85 mg terlipressin, equivalent to 1 mg terlipressin acetate; these mass expressions must not be mistaken for different vial doses. Reconstitute a vial with 5 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and inspect the solution. A peripheral or central line can be used without a dedicated central line; flush afterward. International consensus infusion and titration protocols differ from this US labeled bolus schedule.

bodies.heading: Adjust the US regimen on day 4
bodies.body: Compare day-4 creatinine with the pretreatment dosing baseline. If it has fallen by at least 30%, continue 0.85 mg every 6 hours. If it is below baseline but the decline is less than 30%, the dose may be increased to 1.7 mg every 6 hours after safety assessment. If it is at or above baseline, discontinue rather than escalating. A fall from 3.0 to 2.1 mg/dL is (3.0 − 2.1) ÷ 3.0 × 100 = 30%, so the continuation branch applies. The US day-4 30% rule is distinct from the consensus 25% titration criterion and the SBP PMN-response rule.

bodies.heading: Monitor and stop treatment promptly
bodies.body: Use continuous pulse oximetry and regular respiratory assessment while following creatinine, urine output, blood pressure, volume and ischemic symptoms. Discontinue TERLIVAZ if SpO₂ falls below 90% or hypoxia, increased respiratory symptoms or ischemia develops; a creatinine response does not cancel these safety rules. Manage overload by reassessing albumin and other fluids and adjusting treatment with the team. Under the US label, continue only until 24 hours after the second of two consecutive creatinine values ≤1.5 mg/dL, at least 2 hours apart, or a maximum of 14 days. The consensus also calls for stopping for severe adverse reactions, need for kidney replacement therapy or failure on maximum tolerated therapy; do not combine its different response endpoints into one dosing algorithm.

bodies.heading: Protect the transplant pathway
bodies.body: Pharmacologic improvement can bridge to kidney recovery or liver transplantation but does not cure advanced cirrhosis. Coordinate timely transplant evaluation regardless of vasoconstrictor response; respiratory failure or ischemia can jeopardize candidacy. Kidney replacement therapy is individualized to complications, trajectory and goals, and can provide a bridge for transplant candidates. Arrange liver and kidney follow-up after AKI with medication reconciliation, kidney recovery assessment and a plan to prevent another insult. Discuss symptom relief and goals of care alongside disease-directed treatment.

check.question: A patient receiving TERLIVAZ has improving creatinine but new dyspnea and an SpO₂ of 88%. Which action is best?
choices: Discontinue TERLIVAZ and urgently assess respiratory and volume status.
Continue because kidney improvement overrides the oxygen threshold.
Give more albumin automatically without assessing volume.
Wait until day 4 before responding to hypoxia.
check.rationale: The US label requires discontinuation when SpO₂ falls below 90% and with hypoxia or increased respiratory symptoms. Improving creatinine does not override respiratory safety. Assess oxygenation, volume and other causes urgently; albumin must be reassessed rather than automatically increased.

cirrhosis-decompensated-057.question: Creatinine rises from 0.8 to 1.1 mg/dL within 48 hours in a patient with cirrhosis. Which interpretation is best?
choices: The 0.3 mg/dL rise meets an AKI criterion; its cause still needs evaluation.
AKI is excluded because creatinine remains below 1.5 mg/dL.
The change proves HRS-AKI without volume or source assessment.
The rise is 50%, so only the relative-rise criterion is met.
cirrhosis-decompensated-057.rationale: The absolute rise is 1.1 − 0.8 = 0.3 mg/dL, which meets the 48-hour AKI criterion. The relative rise is 0.3 ÷ 0.8 = 37.5%, not 50%. Low creatinine can be misleading in cirrhosis; the AKI phenotype requires further evaluation.

cirrhosis-decompensated-058.question: A patient with cirrhosis, ascites and AKI is euvolemic after assessment. Is a routine 48-hour albumin infusion required before considering HRS-AKI?
choices: No; current criteria use prompt clinical assessment and response to resuscitation when it is indicated.
Yes; every patient must receive albumin for 48 hours regardless of volume.
Yes; fluid overload makes the diagnostic albumin infusion mandatory.
No; AKI alone proves HRS without evaluating alternative causes.
cirrhosis-decompensated-058.rationale: ADQI-ICA 2024 recommends against systematic 48-hour albumin as a diagnostic prerequisite. Assess volume and alternative causes. When volume resuscitation is clinically indicated, absence of improvement within 24 hours contributes to the HRS-AKI criteria; euvolemia does not prove the diagnosis by itself.

cirrhosis-decompensated-059.question: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites has pre-existing diabetic CKD and new AKI. Which diagnostic approach is best?
choices: Evaluate competing causes and consider superimposed HRS-AKI or mixed injury.
Exclude HRS-AKI solely because CKD existed before admission.
Diagnose HRS-AKI solely from the cirrhosis history.
Treat proteinuria as proof that no hemodynamic component can coexist.
cirrhosis-decompensated-059.rationale: Pre-existing CKD, proteinuria or tubular injury does not automatically exclude HRS-AKI in current consensus criteria. Determine the predominant explanation and assess possible coexistence. Neither cirrhosis nor CKD alone defines the acute cause.

cirrhosis-decompensated-060.question: Which decision creates the greatest avoidable risk when evaluating AKI in cirrhosis?
choices: Label every creatinine rise as HRS without evaluating shock, obstruction or nephrotoxic exposure.
Assess volume and treat true depletion when indicated.
Investigate infection and review medications promptly.
Consider HRS-AKI alongside other causes and revise the assessment with new evidence.
cirrhosis-decompensated-060.rationale: HRS-AKI requires a clinical evaluation and no strong evidence for another primary explanation. Shock, obstruction and drug-related injury may require different urgent care. Volume assessment, infection treatment, medication review and reconsideration of mixed causes support the diagnostic process.

cirrhosis-decompensated-061.question: An adult with suspected HRS-AKI has worsening respiratory symptoms and SpO₂ of 88%. Which TERLIVAZ decision is best?
choices: Do not initiate during hypoxia; urgently evaluate oxygenation and the clinical cause.
Start immediately because HRS removes the respiratory contraindication.
Start if albumin is given first, regardless of oxygenation.
Start without oximetry because respiratory monitoring is optional.
cirrhosis-decompensated-061.rationale: The US label contraindicates TERLIVAZ during hypoxia or worsening respiratory symptoms; SpO₂ below 90% is an explicit safety threshold. Assess volume and respiratory status and discuss suitable alternatives. Albumin and HRS severity do not remove the contraindication.

cirrhosis-decompensated-062.question: On day 4 of US TERLIVAZ therapy, creatinine is unchanged from its pretreatment baseline. Which labeled dose decision applies?
choices: Discontinue TERLIVAZ rather than escalating the dose.
Automatically double the dose because the decline is less than 30%.
Continue indefinitely until creatinine improves.
Use the SBP PMN 25% rule to decide the dose.
cirrhosis-decompensated-062.rationale: The day-4 stop branch takes priority when creatinine is at or above the pretreatment baseline. Dose increase may be considered only when creatinine is below baseline but has fallen less than 30%. International consensus titration and SBP cell-count rules are different pathways.

cirrhosis-decompensated-063.question: Pretreatment creatinine is 3.0 mg/dL and day-4 creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL on US TERLIVAZ. Safety assessment permits continued treatment. Which decision is best?
choices: Continue 0.85 mg IV every 6 hours because creatinine has fallen exactly 30%.
Increase to 1.7 mg every 6 hours because a 30% fall is insufficient.
Discontinue because creatinine remains above 1.5 mg/dL.
Continue for at least 30 days regardless of response.
cirrhosis-decompensated-063.rationale: The decline is (3.0 − 2.1) ÷ 3.0 × 100 = 30%. A decrease of at least 30% meets the US day-4 continuation branch. Continue safety monitoring and apply the labeled success and maximum-duration stopping rules; remaining above 1.5 mg/dL alone is not the day-4 failure rule.

cirrhosis-decompensated-064.question: Which proposal creates the greatest avoidable risk when selecting TERLIVAZ?
choices: Start it despite ongoing mesenteric ischemia because kidney failure is severe.
Assess baseline oxygenation and volume before treatment.
Avoid use during hypoxia and review alternatives with specialists.
Coordinate transplant evaluation and watch for ischemic symptoms during therapy.
cirrhosis-decompensated-064.rationale: Ongoing mesenteric, coronary or peripheral ischemia is a labeled contraindication. Vasoconstriction can cause further ischemic harm, and treatment should stop if ischemic adverse reactions develop. Respiratory assessment and transplant-aware monitoring are necessary parts of care.

metadataAndFigure.review: Summary, concepts, application and key points match the full lesson. Figure labels show cause, volume, treatment and oxygen assessment without presenting routine albumin as a mandatory diagnostic step.

discrepancies.issue: Book lists albumin, midodrine and octreotide without newer preferred treatment ranking.
discrepancies.resolution: Preserve combination as a fallback; explain terlipressin eligibility and monitored norepinephrine alternative from current authorized consensus.

discrepancies.issue: AASLD 2021 Figure 4 includes two-day albumin assessment; 2024 consensus rejects systematic 48-hour albumin as a prerequisite.
discrepancies.resolution: Teach prompt phenotype/volume assessment and lack of improvement within 24 hours after clinically indicated resuscitation; avoid obligatory fluid in euvolemia or overload.

discrepancies.issue: Older functional-only framing can imply structural injury or CKD excludes HRS.
discrepancies.resolution: Teach coexisting CKD, proteinuria or tubular injury while seeking strong evidence for an alternative primary cause.

discrepancies.issue: Consensus uses 25% titration thresholds and international infusion regimens, whereas US FDA labeling uses day-4 30% branches.
discrepancies.resolution: US product dosing follows June 2026 FDA label; explicitly separate consensus pathways.

discrepancies.issue: A less-than-30% decline includes no decline mathematically, but the FDA chart separately stops at or above baseline.
discrepancies.resolution: Give the stop branch priority; permit consideration of escalation only if creatinine is below baseline.

discrepancies.issue: One US vial is 0.85 mg terlipressin but equivalent to 1 mg terlipressin acetate.
discrepancies.resolution: Explain mass equivalence; do not confuse formulation expressions or silently import international dose units.

discrepancies.issue: Diagnostic, SBP, post-paracentesis and treatment albumin regimens differ.
discrepancies.resolution: Individualize 20-40 g/day treatment guidance and withhold for overload; do not import SBP or per-liter dosing.

discrepancies.issue: Consensus renal recovery endpoint differs from FDA treatment endpoint; its narrative and Table 2 also differ in failure duration.
discrepancies.resolution: Use explicit FDA success/max-duration rules for TERLIVAZ, state qualitative specialist stopping indications from consensus, and do not combine different algorithms.
